t: 2119. A Number After a Double Reversal
o: Reverse the digits of num twice and compare with the original. Leading zeros dropped in the first reversal are the only thing that can break equality: e.g. 1800 -> 81 -> 18 != 1800. Any number not ending in 0 survives both reversals unchanged, and 0 maps to itself. Constraints are tiny, so direct simulation is fine, but the trailing-zero observation gives an O(1) answer.
k: Double reversal is the identity unless the first reversal drops trailing zeros.
So the answer is true iff num == 0 or num does not end in 0.

a.i: Apply the digit-reversal operation twice and compare with the input — a direct transcription of the statement.
s: Write rev(x) that pops digits and builds the reversed number.
a.t: O(d) where d is the digit count — two reversal passes

a.i: Only numbers ending in 0 lose information on reversal (except 0 itself, which reverses to 0). Everything else is fixed by a double reversal.
s: Return true if num is 0 or num % 10 != 0, else false.

w: Lead with the O(1) insight; simulation is the fallback if you forget it. Edge cases: num = 0 (true) and multiples of 10 greater than 0 (false). Follow-up: generalize to k reversals — same criterion.
